nameStory: Redtop panicgrass gets its name from the reddish or purplish tinge that often colors the top portions of its flower clusters, especially as they mature. The 'panic' part comes from 'panicle,' a botanical term for the branched, open flower cluster that looks a bit like an upside-down Christmas tree. This red-topped appearance makes it stand out among other grasses in late summer meadows.
description: Redtop panicgrass is a native perennial grass that forms small clumps or patches in open areas throughout New England. It typically grows 2-4 feet tall with narrow, pointed leaves and distinctive branched flower clusters at the top. The whole plant has a somewhat stiff, upright appearance, and the seed heads often develop attractive reddish or purplish tones that catch the eye from a distance.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Open, branched flower clusters (panicles) that are 4-8 inches long and often develop a reddish or purplish tint, especially on the branch tips. The tiny individual flowers are less than 1/8 inch long and feel papery when mature.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Narrow, grass-like leaves that are 4-8 inches long and about 1/4 inch wide, with a prominent white midrib running down the center. Leaves feel somewhat rough and sandpapery when you run your finger along the edges.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms small tufts or clumps rather than spreading into large colonies, with several upright stems growing together. The whole plant has a stiff, rigid appearance that holds its shape even in wind.

idTips.label: Seeds
idTips.description: Tiny, oval seeds that are shiny and dark brown to black when mature, about 1/16 inch long. They fall easily from the seed head when ripe and feel smooth and hard between your fingers.

habitat: Look for redtop panicgrass in sunny, open areas like old fields, meadows, prairie remnants, and woodland edges throughout New England. It prefers well-drained soils and can tolerate both sandy and clay conditions, often growing alongside other native grasses and wildflowers. You'll commonly find it in areas that were once disturbed but are now recovering naturally.

seasonality.spring: New green shoots emerge in late spring, forming small tufts of narrow leaves. The plant is mostly foliage at this stage and easily overlooked among other grasses.
seasonality.summer: Flower clusters begin appearing in mid to late summer, starting out green and gradually developing their characteristic reddish tinge. This is the best time to spot and identify the plant.
seasonality.fall: Seed heads turn deep red to purple and become quite showy, making this the most photogenic season. Seeds ripen and begin dropping by early fall.
seasonality.winter: Dried stems and seed heads persist through winter, turning tan to light brown but still maintaining their distinctive branched structure.

funFact: Despite being called 'rigid' in its scientific name (rigidula), this grass is actually quite flexible and was traditionally used by some Native American groups to weave small baskets and mats because the stems bend without breaking when properly prepared.
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other panicgrasses, but the reddish flower clusters and relatively small, clumping growth habit help distinguish it. Remember: 'Red on top, rigid and small' - it doesn't spread into large colonies like many other grasses.
contextualKnowledge: The genus name Coleataenia is relatively new - this grass was previously classified in the genus Panicum, so you might find it listed as Panicum rigidulum in older field guides. The reclassification happened as scientists better understood the relationships between different grass species using DNA analysis.
compareHints: Long-leaved redtop panicgrass (Coleataenia longifolia) is taller and has longer, wider leaves as its name suggests, typically growing 3-5 feet tall compared to redtop panicgrass's 2-4 feet. The flower clusters of long-leaved are also larger and more open, while redtop panicgrass has more compact, denser flower heads. Both develop reddish tones, but long-leaved tends to be more consistently green.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Compared to its close relative Redtop Panicgrass, Long-leaved Redtop-Panicgrass has distinctly longer and narrower leaves that are more ribbon-like in appearance.
